component_claim: Skill format & progressive disclosure (3-level metadata->body->bundled files)
title: Equipping agents for the real world with Agent Skills
org_author: Anthropic (Barry Zhang, Keith Lazuka, Mahesh Murag)
quote_or_paraphrase: "At startup, the agent pre-loads the name and description of every installed skill into its system prompt." Because the skill's body and bundled files are read only when needed rather than all at once: "the amount of context that can be bundled into a skill is effectively unbounded."
caveats: Anthropic-specific product description (Claude/Claude Code); describes the mechanism our SKILL.md discovery layer reuses, not a routing-to-subagent composition. The 'effectively unbounded' claim is about the content bundled within a single skill (because it need not be read into context up front), not about the number of skills that can be installed; every installed skill's name/description metadata still loads into the system prompt at startup, which is a real (if typically small) per-skill cost.

component_claim: Subagent isolated context window, tool restriction, model-cost routing, and per-agent model/tools/skills preload on one definition
title: Create custom subagents
quote_or_paraphrase: "Each subagent runs in its own context window with a custom system prompt, specific tool access, and independent permissions... Control costs by routing tasks to faster, cheaper models like Haiku." Supported frontmatter fields table lists `tools` ("Tools the subagent can use... To preload Skills into context, use the `skills` field rather than listing `Skill` here"), `model` ("Model to use: `sonnet`, `opus`, `haiku`, `fable`, a full model ID... or `inherit`"), and `skills` ("Skills to preload into the subagent's context at startup. The full skill content is injected, not only the description. Subagents can still invoke unlisted project, user, and plugin skills through the Skill tool") as three fields on the same YAML frontmatter block.
caveats: Describes Claude Code's own subagent feature, not a skill-triggered subagent composition specifically; explicitly names 'faster, cheaper models like Haiku' as a stated benefit. IMPORTANT: this is a second, independently documented schema (alongside GitHub Copilot's `customAgents`, row 29) combining a per-agent `model` override, a `tools` allowlist, and a static `skills` preload of full skill content on one subagent definition - Claude Code and GitHub Copilot are equivalent prior art on this specific point, not GitHub-only. As with GitHub's `skills` field, Claude Code's `skills` frontmatter field is a static list set by whoever defines the subagent and eagerly injects full skill content at startup; it is not the relevance-triggered, progressive-disclosure mechanism (metadata first, body on demand) that defines Agent Skills' discovery/trigger role in Anthropic's own Agent Skills docs (row 1).

component_claim: GitHub Copilot custom-agent config schema documents a per-agent `model` override and a per-agent `skills` preload on the same agent object, alongside the `tools` allowlist
title: Custom agents and sub-agent orchestration
quote_or_paraphrase: Configuration reference table: "model | string | | Model identifier to use while this agent runs" and "skills | string[] | | Skill names to preload into the agent's context at startup." Body text: "Set `model` and `reasoningEffort` to override the parent session's model settings while a custom agent runs." "Per-agent skills" section: "When specified, the full content of each listed skill is eagerly injected into the agent's context at startup-the agent doesn't need to invoke a skill tool; the instructions are already present. Skills are opt-in: agents receive no skills by default, and sub-agents do not inherit skills from the parent."
caveats: This is one of two directly documented schemas found in this research combining a cheaper/different model, a narrow tool allowlist, and skill content on one subagent definition - the other is Claude Code's subagent frontmatter (row 3), which independently supports the same `model`/`tools`/`skills` combination and states that skill content is fully injected at startup. GitHub Copilot is not uniquely positioned on this point; corrects an earlier draft of this report that stated GitHub's custom-agent docs said nothing about per-agent model override. IMPORTANT CAVEAT: the `skills` field is a static list configured by whoever defines the agent, eagerly injecting full skill content at agent-definition time; it is not the relevance-triggered, progressive-disclosure mechanism (metadata loads first, body loads only if triggered) that defines Agent Skills in Anthropic's docs or in GitHub Copilot's own separate 'About agent skills' feature (row 31). No evidence was found that a `customAgents` entry's `skills` list, or a Claude Code subagent's `skills` field, is itself driven by an outer Skill's runtime discovery/trigger decision.

component_claim: Google ADK `task`/`single_turn`-mode subagents run in an isolated session branch and cannot see peer agents' events

When these agents operate in parallel, each agent only sees events from its own branch when building context for AI model calls, and cannot see what its peer agents are doing. Once all parallel branches complete, the parent agent receives the collected results and can proceed."
caveats: Corrects an earlier draft of this report that omitted Google ADK from the isolated-context-window prior art list (§4, §8). This isolation is documented specifically for `task` and `single_turn` collaboration modes. The cited page describes `chat` as full interaction with manual return but does not state whether `chat` uses an isolated session branch, so no isolation claim is made for that mode.

The Agent Skills specification is an open standard, used by a range of different AI systems." GitHub's docs still describe skills and custom agents as two separate features on separate pages; no GitHub source found names a single composed 'skill triggers subagent' pattern.

component_claim: Google ADK Skills: agent-level SkillToolset with metadata-first (L1) discovery, triggered instructions (L2), and on-demand resources (L3) — a Skill-equivalent progressive-disclosure mechanism, documented separately from ADK's coordinator/subagent delegation modes (row 14, row 30)
title: Skills for ADK agents
pub_date: Added 2026-02-13 (docs: Add documentation for Skills support, PR google/adk-docs#1313); page most recently revised 2026-07-24 per commit history; accessed 2026-07-28
quote_or_paraphrase: "An agent Skill is a self-contained unit of functionality that an ADK agent can use to perform a specific task. An agent Skill encapsulates the necessary instructions, resources, and tools required for a task, based on the Agent Skill specification. The structure of a Skill allows it to be loaded incrementally to minimize the impact on the operating context window of the agent." Skill structure: "L1 (Metadata): Provides metadata for skill discovery. This information is defined in the frontmatter section of the SKILL.md file and includes properties such as the Skill name and description." "L2 (Instructions): Contains the primary instructions for the Skill, loaded when the Skill is triggered by the agent. This information is defined in the body of the SKILL.md file." "L3 (Resources): Includes additional resources such as reference materials, assets, and scripts that can be loaded as needed." System instructions: "You must use the load_skill tool to read a skill's instructions before using it... You must use the load_skill_resource tool to view files within a skill's directory."
caveats: Corrects an earlier draft of this report, which stated no Skill-equivalent progressive-disclosure mechanism was found documented for Google ADK; ADK in fact documents one via its SkillToolset (`list_skills`/`load_skill`/`load_skill_resource`), matching Anthropic's L1/L2/L3 metadata->body->resources model closely. IMPORTANT: this Skill mechanism augments the SAME agent's own tool list; it is a single-agent context-loading feature, not a mechanism that invokes a separate subagent. No evidence was found that loading/triggering a Skill here causes ADK's separately documented coordinator/subagent delegation modes (row 14; isolated-session-branch behavior in row 30) to be invoked — the two remain two distinct, separately documented ADK features on separate doc pages, the same pattern already noted for Anthropic, LangChain, and GitHub Copilot (§4, §8).

component_claim: CrewAI Skills: SKILL.md format with progressive disclosure via a discovery stage (name/description/frontmatter) then an activation stage (full body load); Agent objects independently document combinable `llm`, `skills`, and `tools` attributes
title: Skills; Agents
pub_date: Skills page substantially rewritten 2026-03-31 (crewAIInc/crewAI PR #5189, merged); current as of CrewAI v1.15.8, released 2026-07-28; accessed 2026-07-28
quote_or_paraphrase: "Skills are self-contained directories that provide agents with domain-specific instructions, guidelines, and reference material. Each skill is defined by a SKILL.md file with YAML frontmatter and a markdown body... When activated, a skill's instructions are injected directly into the agent's task prompt." "How Skills Are Loaded" section: "Skills use progressive disclosure - only loading what's needed at each stage", table listing "Discovery | Name, description, frontmatter fields | discover_skills()" and "Activation | Full SKILL.md body text | activate_skill()." The companion Agents concepts page lists "LLM (optional) | llm | Union[str, LLM, Any] | Language model that powers the agent" as an independent per-agent attribute, and the Skills page's "Skills + Tools" pattern shows one `Agent()` call setting both `skills=[...]` and `tools=[...]` together.
caveats: Extends the characterization of row 20 (CrewAI Agents page), which stated CrewAI does not document a skill-style progressive-disclosure discovery layer; the dedicated Skills page does, via a `discover_skills()` (metadata) / `activate_skill()` (full body) two-stage API that CrewAI's own docs label "progressive disclosure." IMPORTANT CAVEAT, to avoid overcorrecting: CrewAI's own docs state that "During normal agent execution (passing directory paths via `skills=["./skills"]`), skills are automatically discovered and activated. The progressive loading only matters when using the programmatic API" — so in the common `Agent(skills=[...])` usage, all listed skills are eagerly activated at construction time (a static preload, like Claude Code's and GitHub Copilot's `skills` fields, rows 3 and 29), not triggered one-at-a-time by runtime relevance. No evidence was found that a CrewAI skill's discovery/activation decides, at runtime, to invoke a different, cheaper-model agent; `allow_delegation` (row 20) is a separate, independently configured mechanism not documented as wired to skill activation.

component_claim: Deep Agents harness bundles subagent delegation, progressive-disclosure Skills, a virtual-filesystem/artifact-write toolset, and context management into one agent-creation API
title: Deep Agents overview
quote_or_paraphrase: "Connect to your data: Load memories, skills, and domain knowledge at the right moment" and "Parallelize tasks: Delegate to general or specialized subagents running in isolated context windows" (built-in capabilities list); "Skills package specialized workflows, domain knowledge, and custom instructions for your deep agent... Deep Agents load skills with progressive disclosure: the agent reads SKILL.md frontmatter at startup, then reads full skill content only when a task needs it. This keeps startup context compact while still making rich capabilities available on demand."; "Isolation: Subagents quarantine heavy subtasks and return only final results (see Delegation)."
caveats: Deep Agents is a standalone harness library ("built on top of LangChain's core building blocks for agents"), distinct from the base `langchain` package's own separately documented Subagents/Skills patterns (row 18, row 19); see row 37 for the base library's own first-party pointer to Deep Agents as the harness that bundles both. This is the report's foregrounded closest comparator — see row 35 for the SubAgent schema that combines model/tools/skills/structured-return on one definition.

component_claim: Deep Agents SubAgent definition combines a per-subagent `model` override, a minimal/overridden `tools` allowlist, isolated per-subagent `skills` (not visible to the parent, and vice versa), and a structured `response_format` returned to the parent as JSON
title: Subagents
quote_or_paraphrase: SubAgent field table: "`tools` ... Optional. Tools the subagent can use. Keep this minimal and include only what's needed. Inherits from main agent by default. When specified, overrides the inherited tools entirely." "`model` ... Optional. Overrides the main agent's model. Omit to use the main agent's model. Inherits from main agent by default." "`skills` ... Optional. Skills source paths. When specified, the subagent will load skills from these directories... This allows subagents to have different skill sets than the main agent. Does not inherit from main agent. Only the general-purpose subagent inherits the main agent's skills. When a subagent has skills, it runs its own independent SkillsMiddleware instance. Skill state is fully isolated—a subagent's loaded skills are not visible to the parent, and vice versa." "`response_format` ... Optional. Structured output schema for the subagent. When set, the parent receives the subagent's result as JSON instead of free-form text." Also: "Subagents solve the context bloat problem. When agents use tools with large outputs... the main agent receives only the final result, not the dozens of tool calls that produced it."
caveats: The most complete single-schema composition found in this research: one subagent definition combines a cheaper/different model, a narrow tool allowlist, isolated skill content, and a structured compact return — exceeding the model+tools+skills combination documented by Claude Code (row 3), GitHub Copilot (row 29), and CrewAI (row 33) by additionally isolating skill visibility and supporting a structured JSON return. component_claim: Microsoft Agent Framework's own Handoff orchestration docs explicitly contrast Handoff (full context/ownership transfer between agents, no central authority) against Agent-as-Tools (primary agent retains ownership and control returns after each subtask) as two fundamentally different control-flow patterns

In contrast, agent-as-tools involves a primary agent that delegates sub tasks to other agents and once the agent completes the sub task, control returns to the primary agent."
